sentences.text: This animal belongs to the genus Gorgosaurus, which is placed in the subfamily Albertosaurinae within the family Tyrannosauridae.
Adult individuals measured between 8 and 9 meters in length and had a body mass of 2 to 3 metric tons.
It possessed dozens of large, sharp teeth in its jaws, with the largest known skull reaching 99 centimeters in length.
The creature also had small, two-fingered forelimbs.
The genus was established and described by Lawrence Lambe in 1914.
The holotype specimen, a nearly complete skeleton with a skull designated NMC 2120, was discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.
As an apex predator, Gorgosaurus preyed on abundant ceratopsids and hadrosaurs.
Therrien and colleagues proposed in 2021 that the maximum bite force of adult albertosaurines like Gorgosaurus was around 12,200 to 21,800 newtons.

Phil Currie originally described Gorgosaurus skin as essentially smooth and lacking scales, similar to large modern birds, though some isolated patches show denser, larger scales comparable to those of a Gila monster.
Gorgosaurus is sometimes considered a junior synonym of Albertosaurus because Albertosaurus was named first.
Gorgosaurus lived in western North America during the Late Cretaceous (Campanian) between approximately 76.5 and 73 million years ago.
It inhabited a lush floodplain environment near the edge of an inland sea.
Specifically, Gorgosaurus libratus lived between 76.6 and 75.1 million years ago during the middle Campanian stage.
It is debated whether the genus Deinodon represents a distinct animal or is synonymous with Gorgosaurus due to the uniformity of tyrannosaurid teeth.
Skeletons from the Two Medicine and Judith River Formations in Montana likely belong to Gorgosaurus, but it is uncertain if they are G. libratus or a new species.
The specimen previously named Gorgosaurus lancensis was renamed Nanotyrannus in 1988, and while it was once thought to be a juvenile Tyrannosaurus, it is now considered a valid taxon.
Specimens previously assigned to Gorgosaurus from Mongolia are now considered to be juveniles of Tarbosaurus bataar.
